documents.title: Allostatic load-cardiovascular disease associations and the mediating effect of inflammatory factors: a prospective cohort study
documents.text:
Which population and incident outcomes were analyzed?
The analytic cohort comprised 205,504 participants and 18,542 incident CVD events during an article-reported 13-year follow-up period. The analytic sample is not the entire UK Biobank recruitment population. The reported 13-year period is not described here as a mean or median follow-up.

documents.title: Allostatic load-cardiovascular disease associations and the mediating effect of inflammatory factors: a prospective cohort study
documents.text:
What does the allostatic-load score represent?
Allostatic load was operationalized using 12 baseline biomarkers with quartile-based risk scoring and a score range of 0–12. HDL and IGF-1 used the low-value risk direction. This biomarker score is not a direct measurement of psychological stress, a neuroendocrine response or an inflammatory intervention.

documents.title: Allostatic load-cardiovascular disease associations and the mediating effect of inflammatory factors: a prospective cohort study
documents.text:
What was the adjusted high-versus-zero AL association?
In adjusted Model 3, AL ≥6 versus AL = 0 was associated with incident CVD at HR 2.15 (95% CI 1.99–2.33). AL = 0 is the reference group. This relative hazard association is not a 115% absolute-risk increase or a treatment effect.

documents.title: Allostatic load-cardiovascular disease associations and the mediating effect of inflammatory factors: a prospective cohort study
documents.text:
What do the nonlinear and sensitivity analyses add?
The AL–CVD association was nonlinear, and the main text reported directionally similar results after excluding events in the first three years after baseline. No additional precise hazard ratios from supplementary tables are supplied here, and this sensitivity analysis does not fully exclude reverse causation.

documents.title: Allostatic load-cardiovascular disease associations and the mediating effect of inflammatory factors: a prospective cohort study
documents.text:
Does the mediation estimate establish prevention by lowering neutrophils?
Eight candidate mediators entered the correlation analysis; the neutrophil-count mediation estimate was 4.73%. This is model-based decomposition using baseline indicators, not a proven causal pathway or evidence that lowering neutrophils or an inflammatory marker prevents CVD.

documents.title: Allostatic load-cardiovascular disease associations and the mediating effect of inflammatory factors: a prospective cohort study
documents.text:
What prospective cohort evidence links allostatic load to incident CVD?
An analytic cohort of 205,504 participants had 18,542 incident CVD events during the article-reported 13-year period; Model 3 compared AL ≥6 with AL = 0 at HR 2.15 (95% CI 1.99–2.33). These are observational relative-hazard findings, not a treatment effect.

documents.title: Allostatic load-cardiovascular disease associations and the mediating effect of inflammatory factors: a prospective cohort study
documents.text:
How was a multisystem biomarker AL score operationalized?
Twelve baseline biomarkers formed a 0–12 score using quartile-based risk scoring, with the low-value direction for HDL and IGF-1. It is not a direct psychological-stress measure or an intervention.

documents.title: Allostatic load-cardiovascular disease associations and the mediating effect of inflammatory factors: a prospective cohort study
documents.text:
Was the AL–CVD association nonlinear and examined in sensitivity analyses?
Nonlinearity P<0.001 and directionally similar results after excluding first-three-year events were reported in the main text. This does not fully exclude reverse causation.

What statistical inflammatory mediation was reported?
Among eight candidate mediators in the correlation analysis, the neutrophil-count mediation estimate was 4.73%. Baseline model decomposition does not establish a causal pathway or drug benefit.

documents.title: Circadian Immunity and Vascular Inflammation in Cardiovascular Disease Chronotherapy Windows: Time for a Re-Assessment
documents.text: How do circadian clock disruption and time-of-day biology interact with immune-cell trafficking, inflammatory signaling and vascular homeostasis across cardiovascular diseases, and what level of evidence supports translating these rhythms into cardiovascular chronotherapy?

documents.title: Circadian Immunity and Vascular Inflammation in Cardiovascular Disease Chronotherapy Windows: Time for a Re-Assessment
documents.text:
Narrative review of circadian immune-vascular mechanisms across cardiovascular disease, distinguishing preclinical chronotherapy rationale from heterogeneous and unresolved clinical timing evidence; no new data were created or analyzed.
This narrative review synthesizes experimental, mechanistic, epidemiological and clinical literature linking the circadian clock to cardiovascular immune and inflammatory biology. It organizes evidence around the CLOCK-BMAL1 transcriptional network, PER/CRY feedback, REV-ERB/ROR regulation, redox-sensitive signaling, NF-kB and NLRP3 inflammasome activity, cytokine and chemokine rhythms, and time-dependent immune-cell trafficking. These mechanisms are discussed across atherosclerosis, stroke, ischemic heart disease and heart failure. The review further evaluates preclinical chronotherapeutic strategies targeting clock and inflammatory pathways and contrasts them with a more limited and heterogeneous clinical evidence base. It does not report new experimental or clinical data, perform a meta-analysis, establish a universal cardiovascular dosing schedule, or demonstrate clinical efficacy for experimental clock-targeting compounds.

documents.title: Circadian Immunity and Vascular Inflammation in Cardiovascular Disease Chronotherapy Windows: Time for a Re-Assessment
documents.text:
The review places CLOCK-BMAL1, PER/CRY and REV-ERB/ROR feedback loops at the center of temporal regulation of cardiovascular immune biology.
This is a synthesis of prior molecular and experimental literature rather than a new clock experiment.
Core clock machinery
BMAL1/ARNTL, CLOCK, PER1/2/3, CRY1/2, REV-ERB alpha/beta and ROR alpha/gamma are integrated with redox and epigenetic regulation.
Sections 2.1-2.4; Figures 1-2; Tables 1-2.

documents.title: Circadian Immunity and Vascular Inflammation in Cardiovascular Disease Chronotherapy Windows: Time for a Re-Assessment
documents.text:
Circadian timing is synthesized as a regulator of PRR, NF-kB and NLRP3 inflammatory signaling and of cytokine, chemokine and adhesion-molecule rhythms.
These mechanisms derive from heterogeneous experimental systems and should not be represented as one fully demonstrated causal human pathway.
Inflammatory networks
The review discusses IL-1beta, IL-6, IL-18, TNF-alpha, CCL2, CXCL12, ICAM1, VCAM1 and related inflammatory networks.
Sections 3-4; Figure 3; Table 3.

documents.title: Circadian Immunity and Vascular Inflammation in Cardiovascular Disease Chronotherapy Windows: Time for a Re-Assessment
documents.text:
The review describes circadian variation in immune-cell number, trafficking and function across neutrophils, monocytes/macrophages, lymphocytes and dendritic cells.
Timing, phase and mechanisms vary by species, tissue and experimental model.
Trafficking mechanisms
BMAL1, chemokine axes, sympathetic signaling and cell-intrinsic clocks are synthesized as contributors to rhythmic immune trafficking and function.
Section 5; Figures 4-5.

documents.title: Circadian Immunity and Vascular Inflammation in Cardiovascular Disease Chronotherapy Windows: Time for a Re-Assessment
documents.text:
Circadian disruption is reviewed in relation to atherosclerosis, stroke, ischemic heart disease/myocardial infarction and heart failure through overlapping inflammatory, endothelial, metabolic and oxidative-stress mechanisms.
Evidence strength and causality differ materially across disease, mechanism and model.
Disease domains
The synthesis compares atherosclerosis, stroke, ischemic heart disease, myocardial infarction and heart failure rather than reporting one new cross-disease experiment.
Sections 6.1-6.4; Figures 6-8.

documents.title: Circadian Immunity and Vascular Inflammation in Cardiovascular Disease Chronotherapy Windows: Time for a Re-Assessment
documents.text:
Preclinical studies provide a mechanistic rationale for time-dependent intervention targeting clock and inflammatory pathways.
This evidence is predominantly preclinical and must not be converted into human treatment-efficacy claims.
Preclinical strategies
The review discusses REV-ERB agonists, NLRP3 inhibitors, NF-kB pathway modulation, CCR2/CCL2 and CXCL12/CXCR4 strategies.
Section 7.1; Table 4.

documents.title: Circadian Immunity and Vascular Inflammation in Cardiovascular Disease Chronotherapy Windows: Time for a Re-Assessment
documents.text:
Clinical chronotherapy evidence is heterogeneous and does not define a universal optimal dosing time for most cardiovascular drugs.
Physiological timing effects and mechanistic rationale are not equivalent to proven reductions in clinical outcomes.
Drug classes and timing
The review discusses aspirin, beta-blockers, melatonin, tPA, SGLT2 inhibitors, colchicine, ACEIs/ARBs, MRAs, ARNI and antihypertensive timing.
Conflicting trials
Hygia and related studies reported bedtime-dosing benefits, whereas BedMed did not reproduce a cardiovascular-event benefit.
Section 7.2; Table 5.

documents.title: Circadian Immunity and Vascular Inflammation in Cardiovascular Disease Chronotherapy Windows: Time for a Re-Assessment
documents.text:
The review identifies unresolved methodological and translational gaps that limit precision chronotherapy.
These gaps are part of the authors' discussion, not newly experimentally tested findings.
Research gaps
Constitutive-versus-inducible knockout-model differences, immune-cell-subpopulation heterogeneity, insufficient spatiotemporal resolution of vascular-immune interactions and the need for high-quality circadian-aware clinical trials are highlighted.
Sections 8.1-8.4.

documents.title: Circadian Immunity and Vascular Inflammation in Cardiovascular Disease Chronotherapy Windows: Time for a Re-Assessment
documents.text:
Chronotherapy claims in this review require explicit separation of mechanistic rhythmicity, preclinical time-of-day efficacy, human surrogate effects and hard cardiovascular outcomes.
These evidence levels are not interchangeable. Human clinical timing evidence remains incomplete or conflicting for many cardiovascular therapies.
Human timing evidence
Bedtime aspirin can alter morning platelet reactivity, but cardiovascular event reduction has not been established by a large randomized trial; SGLT2-inhibitor and colchicine timing remain insufficiently tested.
Outcome-level uncertainty
Antihypertensive bedtime-dosing studies have reported conflicting cardiovascular outcome results, including the Hygia and BedMed trials.
Section 7.2; Table 5; Sections 8.1-8.4.

documents.title: Circadian Immunity and Vascular Inflammation in Cardiovascular Disease Chronotherapy Windows: Time for a Re-Assessment
documents.text:
What type of article is this?
It is a narrative Review Article synthesizing prior evidence. It reports no new experimental or clinical dataset, systematic study-selection workflow or pooled meta-analysis.

documents.title: Circadian Immunity and Vascular Inflammation in Cardiovascular Disease Chronotherapy Windows: Time for a Re-Assessment
documents.text:
Which circadian clock components are central to cardiovascular immune regulation?
The review centers on CLOCK-BMAL1, PER/CRY and REV-ERB/ROR feedback networks, including redox and epigenetic regulation; these are synthesized from prior work rather than tested as one new experiment.

documents.title: Circadian Immunity and Vascular Inflammation in Cardiovascular Disease Chronotherapy Windows: Time for a Re-Assessment
documents.text:
How does circadian disruption interact with NF-kB and NLRP3?
The review links clock and redox regulation with pattern-recognition receptor, NF-kB and NLRP3 inflammatory signaling, cytokines and chemokines. The underlying models are heterogeneous and do not establish one complete causal pathway in humans.

documents.title: Circadian Immunity and Vascular Inflammation in Cardiovascular Disease Chronotherapy Windows: Time for a Re-Assessment
documents.text:
Which immune cells show circadian trafficking or functional rhythms?
Prior evidence discussed for neutrophils, monocytes/macrophages, lymphocytes and dendritic cells indicates rhythmic numbers, trafficking or function, with phase and mechanism varying across species and tissues.

documents.title: Circadian Immunity and Vascular Inflammation in Cardiovascular Disease Chronotherapy Windows: Time for a Re-Assessment
documents.text:
Which cardiovascular diseases are discussed?
The review discusses atherosclerosis, stroke, ischemic heart disease and myocardial infarction, and heart failure, with hypertension considered in blood-pressure chronotherapy. Evidence strength differs across disease contexts.

documents.title: Circadian Immunity and Vascular Inflammation in Cardiovascular Disease Chronotherapy Windows: Time for a Re-Assessment
documents.text:
Does the review prove that REV-ERB agonists treat cardiovascular disease in humans?
No. REV-ERB agonist chronotherapy is discussed as mechanistic and preclinical rationale, not demonstrated human cardiovascular treatment efficacy.

documents.title: Circadian Immunity and Vascular Inflammation in Cardiovascular Disease Chronotherapy Windows: Time for a Re-Assessment
documents.text:
Should all antihypertensive medications be taken at bedtime?
No. Clinical evidence conflicts: Hygia and related studies reported bedtime-dosing benefits, while BedMed did not reproduce a cardiovascular-event benefit. The review does not support a universal bedtime recommendation.

documents.title: Circadian Immunity and Vascular Inflammation in Cardiovascular Disease Chronotherapy Windows: Time for a Re-Assessment
documents.text:
Does bedtime aspirin have proven myocardial infarction or stroke outcome benefit?
No large randomized trial cited by this review directly establishes reduced overall myocardial infarction or stroke incidence from bedtime aspirin dosing; physiological timing effects do not prove event reduction.

documents.title: Circadian Immunity and Vascular Inflammation in Cardiovascular Disease Chronotherapy Windows: Time for a Re-Assessment
documents.text:
Are SGLT2-inhibitor, colchicine, MRA or ARNI dosing times clinically established?
No. The review discusses these drug classes, but does not establish clinically validated optimal timing or universal cardiovascular outcome benefits for them.

documents.title: Circadian Immunity and Vascular Inflammation in Cardiovascular Disease Chronotherapy Windows: Time for a Re-Assessment
documents.text:
Is this a systematic review or meta-analysis?
No. The article reports no explicit systematic-search strategy, PRISMA study-selection workflow or quantitative meta-analysis; its 392 references are bibliography entries, not a systematic count of independent studies.

documents.title: Circadian Immunity and Vascular Inflammation in Cardiovascular Disease Chronotherapy Windows: Time for a Re-Assessment
documents.text:
What gaps remain before cardiovascular chronotherapy can become precision medicine?
Constitutive-versus-inducible model differences, immune-subpopulation and spatiotemporal heterogeneity, individualized rhythm variation and high-quality circadian-aware clinical trials remain important gaps.

documents.title: Circadian Immunity and Vascular Inflammation in Cardiovascular Disease Chronotherapy Windows: Time for a Re-Assessment
documents.text:
Prior evidence links circadian clock networks with immune and vascular processes, inflammatory and redox pathways.
Immune-cell number, trafficking and functional state can vary with circadian timing across experimental contexts.
Experimental circadian disruption can alter cardiovascular inflammatory phenotypes, while cardiovascular physiology and events exhibit time-of-day patterns.
Preclinical evidence provides a mechanistic rationale for chronotherapy; some cardiovascular drugs show dosing-time-dependent physiological effects.
Clinical chronotherapy remains an active and unresolved translational field.

documents.title: Circadian Immunity and Vascular Inflammation in Cardiovascular Disease Chronotherapy Windows: Time for a Re-Assessment
documents.text:
A new patient cohort, new experimental data or a newly analyzed dataset.
A systematic review, meta-analysis or pooled quantitative effect size.
One universally causal circadian pathway across all cardiovascular diseases.
Human cardiovascular treatment efficacy of REV-ERB agonists or time-targeted NLRP3 or NF-kB inhibition.
Universal superiority of bedtime antihypertensive dosing or a dosing schedule suitable for every patient.
Reduced myocardial infarction or stroke outcomes from bedtime aspirin.
Established optimal dosing for SGLT2 inhibitors, colchicine, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists or ARNI.
A guideline-level recommendation to change cardiovascular medication timing.

documents.title: Circadian Immunity and Vascular Inflammation in Cardiovascular Disease Chronotherapy Windows: Time for a Re-Assessment
documents.text:
This is a narrative, non-systematic evidence synthesis with no new dataset or pooled effect estimate.
Species, tissues, disease models and evidence levels are heterogeneous; causal animal or cell findings cannot automatically be generalized to human cardiovascular disease.
Constitutive and inducible clock-gene knockout models may yield different findings.
Treatment-timing evidence is uneven across cardiovascular drug classes and many proposed chronotherapy windows remain theoretical or preclinical.
Clinical antihypertensive timing evidence is conflicting, including Hygia-versus-BedMed differences.
No universal dosing recommendation is established; high-quality circadian-aware randomized clinical trials are needed.

documents.title: From Disease-Specific Models to Broad Clinical Utility: A Perspective on AI Hybrid Ensemble Frameworks
documents.text:
This methodological Perspective argues for context-sensitive learner integration, evaluation across independent cohorts and cautious interpretation of feature attribution. Its deployment discussion identifies requirements for future clinical translation rather than reporting a newly validated model.
The Perspective connects clinical AI design to the practical demands of evaluating and interpreting ensemble models. It advocates combining complementary learners according to the clinical setting and selecting models through aggregate evaluation across independent cohorts. Its discussion of SHAP emphasizes that feature attributions depend on data distributions and should be considered alongside sensitivity analysis and calibration. Distribution shift, computational resources, standardization and clinical workflow integration frame the translation agenda. On this evidence page, these arguments support methodological choices and limitations discussions; performance estimates and empirical validation claims belong to the cited primary studies, not to this Perspective.

documents.title: System biology analysis reveals circadian rhythm disorder associated with development and progression in colorectal cancer
documents.text: Can a transcriptomic scoring framework derived from colon circadian genes and colorectal-cancer single-cell co-expression structure quantify endogenous circadian misalignment across heterogeneous datasets, capture CRC progression and tumor-microenvironment states, and identify experimentally testable regulators such as SYNE1?

documents.title: System biology analysis reveals circadian rhythm disorder associated with development and progression in colorectal cancer
documents.text:
A multicohort systems-biology study integrating 35 public GEO datasets, a 94,683-cell colorectal-cancer single-cell framework, cross-species circadian perturbation analyses, clinical/transcriptomic cohort evaluation, and CRC-cell experiments to develop ClockProCRC, characterize circadian-misalignment states in colorectal cancer, and prioritize SYNE1 as a functionally tested candidate regulator.
This study developed ClockProCRC as a transcriptomic framework for quantifying endogenous circadian misalignment in colorectal cancer (CRC). The article reports 3,758 samples across 35 public GEO datasets overall. Its primary GSE166555 single-cell cohort comprised 13 CRC tissue samples and 12 normal mucosal samples, yielding 94,683 cells after quality control. A 906-gene colon circadian reference was projected into the CRC single-cell data, followed by KNN meta-cell aggregation and high-dimensional co-expression analysis. Nine circadian modules were identified; four CRC-associated modules (M1, M3, M4 and M6) contributed a 559-gene circadian transcriptional-driver signature. ClockProCRC used expression-matched random-background correction with 100 expression bins and 1,000 random samplings and was evaluated across multiple human, mouse and non-human-primate circadian perturbation datasets. Higher ClockProCRC values were associated with CRC progression, worse survival in the analyzed retrospective cohort, and distinct single-cell microenvironmental states. Gene-regulatory-network analysis prioritized the NFATC2-SYNE1 axis, and SYNE1 silencing in HCT116 and SW480 cells reduced migration, invasion and colony formation while shifting epithelial/mesenchymal marker expression. CLOCK and SYNE1 perturbation experiments further linked ClockProCRC-defined circadian disruption to SYNE1 rhythmicity, with partial molecular restoration after melatonin treatment. The study supports a systems-level circadian framework and an experimentally testable SYNE1 hypothesis, but it does not establish prospective clinical utility, treatment efficacy, or in-vivo therapeutic validation.

documents.title: System biology analysis reveals circadian rhythm disorder associated with development and progression in colorectal cancer
documents.text:
What is ClockProCRC and how was it constructed?
ClockProCRC is a transcriptomic circadian-misalignment scoring framework. The study began with a 906-gene colon circadian reference and separately used CRC single-cell co-expression analysis to derive nine modules and a 559-gene four-module CTD signature. The ClockProCRC scoring Methods then applied expression-matched random-background correction to circadian rhythm disorder genes using 100 expression bins and 1,000 random samplings. The reviewed manuscript text does not establish that the 559 CTD genes are identical to the final scoring gene set.

documents.title: System biology analysis reveals circadian rhythm disorder associated with development and progression in colorectal cancer
documents.text:
How large was the ClockProCRC study?
The Methods reports 3,758 samples across 35 public GEO datasets. The primary GSE166555 single-cell cohort comprised 25 tissue samples (13 CRC and 12 normal mucosa) and retained 94,683 cells after quality control. These are heterogeneous sample, tissue and cell counts and should not be interpreted as 3,758 unique human participants.

documents.title: System biology analysis reveals circadian rhythm disorder associated with development and progression in colorectal cancer
documents.text:
Was ClockProCRC associated with colorectal-cancer progression and survival?
Yes, within the analyzed retrospective/public datasets. ClockProCRC increased across progression-related states from normal mucosa through adenoma/dysplasia and CRC to colorectal liver metastasis, and higher scores were associated with worse overall survival in GSE17537 (n=55; log-rank P<0.01). This is association evidence rather than prospective clinical validation.

documents.title: System biology analysis reveals circadian rhythm disorder associated with development and progression in colorectal cancer
documents.text:
What did the single-cell analysis show about circadian misalignment and the CRC tumor microenvironment?
In GSE200997 and GSE196964, ClockProCRC-defined higher-disruption states were associated with enrichment of epithelial and plasma-cell populations, relative depletion of fibroblast/endothelial populations, and altered intercellular communication including stronger pro-inflammatory signaling patterns. These analyses identify state associations and do not by themselves prove causality.

documents.title: System biology analysis reveals circadian rhythm disorder associated with development and progression in colorectal cancer
documents.text:
Why was SYNE1 prioritized in this study?
SYNE1 emerged from the CTD gene-regulatory-network analysis. Across 100 genetic-algorithm iterations, 61 recurrent regulatory axes were identified, and the NFATC2→SYNE1 relationship showed higher modeled regulatory strength in CRC (0.607; 95% CI 0.412-0.802) than in normal mucosa (-0.102; 95% CI -0.058-0.262). SYNE1 also showed circadian perturbation-associated expression/rhythmicity changes in independent datasets.

documents.title: System biology analysis reveals circadian rhythm disorder associated with development and progression in colorectal cancer
documents.text:
What happened when SYNE1 was knocked down in colorectal-cancer cells?
In HCT116 and SW480 cells, siRNA-mediated SYNE1 knockdown reduced Transwell migration/invasion, reduced wound-healing migration and colony formation, increased E-cadherin and ZO-1, and decreased N-cadherin. These findings support an in-vitro functional role but do not establish in-vivo therapeutic efficacy.

documents.title: System biology analysis reveals circadian rhythm disorder associated with development and progression in colorectal cancer
documents.text:
How did CLOCK knockdown, melatonin and the reported SYNE1 AUC relate to the circadian perturbation experiment?
CLOCK knockdown increased ClockProCRC and disrupted SYNE1 rhythmicity; melatonin partially restored the ClockProCRC-defined state and SYNE1 rhythmicity in CRC-cell experiments. The reported SYNE1 AUC of 0.915 refers specifically to discrimination of CLOCK-knockdown experimental conditions, not to CRC diagnosis or patient-level prediction.

documents.title: System biology analysis reveals circadian rhythm disorder associated with development and progression in colorectal cancer
documents.text:
Are ClockProCRC or SYNE1 clinically validated for diagnosis, prognosis or treatment selection?
No. ClockProCRC has multicohort analytical and retrospective association evidence but lacks large prospective multicenter clinical validation and a universal clinical cutoff. SYNE1 has computational and in-vitro functional evidence but no SYNE1-directed animal efficacy or patient-treatment validation.

documents.title: System biology analysis reveals circadian rhythm disorder associated with development and progression in colorectal cancer
documents.text:
How can transcriptomic data be used to quantify endogenous circadian misalignment in colorectal cancer?
ClockProCRC uses expression-matched background correction with 100 expression bins and 1,000 random samplings to quantify transcriptomic circadian dysregulation.

documents.title: System biology analysis reveals circadian rhythm disorder associated with development and progression in colorectal cancer
documents.text:
What multicohort and single-cell evidence links circadian misalignment with colorectal-cancer progression?
The study integrates a primary 25-sample / 94,683-cell single-cell cohort with multiple public cohorts and reports associations between higher ClockProCRC values and CRC progression-related states.

documents.title: System biology analysis reveals circadian rhythm disorder associated with development and progression in colorectal cancer
documents.text:
Was ClockProCRC evaluated across independent circadian perturbation datasets and species?
The article reports evaluation across 16 independent public datasets spanning human, mouse and non-human-primate circadian contexts.

documents.title: System biology analysis reveals circadian rhythm disorder associated with development and progression in colorectal cancer
documents.text:
Which candidate regulator of circadian dysregulation in CRC was prioritized and functionally tested?
Gene-regulatory-network analyses prioritized the NFATC2-SYNE1 axis, and SYNE1 perturbation was functionally examined in HCT116 and SW480 cells.

documents.title: System biology analysis reveals circadian rhythm disorder associated with development and progression in colorectal cancer
documents.text:
How are ClockProCRC-defined circadian states related to colorectal-cancer tumor-microenvironment composition and signaling?
Single-cell analyses associated ClockProCRC states with differing epithelial, plasma-cell, fibroblast, endothelial and intercellular communication patterns.

documents.title: System biology analysis reveals circadian rhythm disorder associated with development and progression in colorectal cancer
documents.text:
The article defines a 906-gene colon circadian reference and derives CRC-associated circadian co-expression structure from a 94,683-cell single-cell dataset.
ClockProCRC uses expression-matched random-background correction and varies in expected directions across multiple experimentally or behaviorally perturbed circadian datasets.
Higher ClockProCRC values are associated with CRC progression-related states and poorer overall survival in the analyzed retrospective/public cohorts.
ClockProCRC-defined states are associated with distinct CRC single-cell composition and intercellular-communication patterns.
SYNE1 is prioritized by gene-regulatory-network analysis and shows circadian perturbation-associated expression/rhythmicity changes across independent datasets.
SYNE1 knockdown in HCT116 and SW480 cells reduces migration, invasion and colony formation and shifts E-cadherin, ZO-1 and N-cadherin expression.
CLOCK knockdown and melatonin rescue conditions alter ClockProCRC and SYNE1 rhythmicity in CRC-cell experiments.

documents.text:
That ClockProCRC has been prospectively validated in a multicenter clinical cohort.
That ClockProCRC is a clinically approved diagnostic, prognostic, screening or treatment-selection test.
That the cohort-specific median or single-cell 75th-percentile grouping rules define a universal clinical cutoff.
That higher ClockProCRC causally drives CRC progression in humans; most clinical and tumor-microenvironment evidence is observational or retrospective.
That ClockProCRC adds incremental clinical utility over established CRC staging, molecular markers or treatment-response assessment.
That SYNE1 is a validated therapeutic target in patients with CRC.
That SYNE1 inhibition improves tumor control, metastasis or survival in vivo; the study reports cell-line perturbation but no SYNE1-directed animal efficacy experiment.
That melatonin treatment is effective for CRC patients; melatonin was used as a molecular rescue condition in cell experiments.
That AUC=0.915 represents CRC diagnosis or patient-level prediction; it refers to discrimination of CLOCK-knockdown experimental conditions by SYNE1 expression.
That single-cell ligand-receptor and pathway analyses prove causal tumor-microenvironment remodeling.

documents.title: System biology analysis reveals circadian rhythm disorder associated with development and progression in colorectal cancer
documents.text:
Most human clinical evidence derives from retrospective/public transcriptomic datasets rather than a prospectively enrolled multicenter clinical validation cohort.
The study integrates heterogeneous evidence units across human, mouse and non-human-primate datasets; sample, tissue, cohort and cell counts are not interchangeable.
ClockProCRC grouping uses data-context-specific thresholds (75th percentile for single-cell analyses and commonly the cohort median for bulk cohorts), not a universal clinical cutoff.
The manuscript distinguishes the 906-gene colon circadian reference from the 559-gene four-module CTD signature. The ClockProCRC scoring Methods refers to circadian rhythm disorder genes (CRGs), so this evidence page does not infer that the 559 CTD genes are identical to the final score-input gene set.
The Results text contains the accession GSE200977, whereas the Methods and Figure 4 legend identify the CRC single-cell cohort as GSE200997; the evidence page uses GSE200997 and records the Results-text accession as a manuscript typo.
The manuscript contains several wording/locator inconsistencies, including knockdown described once as knockout, Transwell language that conflates proliferation with migration/invasion, and a scratch-assay timing inconsistency; the evidence page follows the experimental Methods and figure legends.
The public ClockProCRC GitHub repository is an associated code resource but does not exactly mirror the accepted manuscript: the README reports an earlier 32-cohort/3,075-sample configuration, the current scoring script defaults to 50 bins rather than the manuscript's 100 bins, and DiffCircadian.R contains a placeholder scoring function.
SYNE1 functional evidence is in vitro; no SYNE1-directed animal efficacy experiment or human therapeutic study is reported.
The publisher currently labels the article as an early peer-reviewed accepted version that may undergo further editing before the final Version of Record.

documents.title: Vascular smooth muscle cell-derived KIF13B inhibits proinflammatory responses to protect against atherosclerosis
documents.text: Does VSMC-derived KIF13B regulate vascular smooth-muscle-cell phenotypic state and experimental plaque stability through KCTD10-dependent KLF4 turnover, and can reducing KLF4 activity rescue the consequences of KIF13B loss in experimental systems? Human plaque findings are associative; causal and intervention evidence is preclinical.

documents.title: Vascular smooth muscle cell-derived KIF13B inhibits proinflammatory responses to protect against atherosclerosis
documents.text:
A mechanistic translational preclinical study combining associative human carotid-plaque evidence with mouse atherosclerosis genetics, pooled single-cell analysis, primary human aortic smooth-muscle-cell perturbation, biochemical rescue and preclinical pharmacology to investigate how KIF13B regulates VSMC state through KCTD10-dependent KLF4 turnover.
This study integrates paired human carotid endarterectomy plaque regions, independent public human transcriptomic, proteomic, methylation and spatial-transcriptomic evidence, VSMC-specific and global mouse Kif13b perturbation, aortic single-cell RNA sequencing, primary human aortic smooth-muscle-cell gain- and loss-of-function experiments, biochemical rescue and preclinical pharmacology. Human observations associate lower KIF13B, particularly in VSMCs, with advanced or unstable plaque features and lower collagen, but do not establish human causality. In male AAV8-PCSK9 mice, VSMC-specific Kif13b deletion increased lesion burden and adverse plaque-composition features without detected differences in plasma total cholesterol or triglycerides in the tested model. Pooled mouse single-cell analysis and primary HASMC perturbation linked KIF13B loss to reduced matrix/collagen programs and increased inflammatory VSMC programs. KLF4 knockdown rescued KIF13B-loss phenotypes in HASMCs. CHX/MG132, ubiquitination, co-immunoprecipitation and KCTD10-overexpression experiments support a model in which KIF13B maintains KCTD10 abundance and KCTD10 promotes KLF4 ubiquitination and proteasomal turnover; how KIF13B controls KCTD10 remains unresolved. Kenpaullone reduced KLF4 promoter activity/expression and rescued cellular and mouse phenotypes in this study, but this is preclinical proof-of-concept. Kenpaullone is not established as a KLF4-selective drug, and no human treatment efficacy was tested.

Lower KIF13B was associated with more advanced or unstable human atherosclerotic plaque states, with prominent differences in VSMCs.
These human tissue and public-dataset observations are associative and do not establish that changing KIF13B alters plaque outcomes in patients.
Local carotid plaques
Six CEA patients contributed paired advanced and adjacent regions; Figure 1 reports lower KIF13B in advanced regions, with scRNA analysis n=4 per condition and protein/histologic analyses n=6 per condition.
GSE120521
KIF13B mRNA was lower in unstable than stable regions from four paired carotid plaques: n=4 stable and n=4 unstable.
PXD062283
KIF13B protein was lower in the JCI stable n=19 versus unstable n=38 plaque comparison.
Plaque matrix relationship
Human plaque analysis showed lower VSMC KIF13B and lower collagen in advanced regions, with a positive association between VSMC KIF13B signal and collagen content.
Epigenetic evidence
Supplementary public-dataset reanalysis associated higher KIF13B methylation with atherosclerotic versus control tissue and symptomatic versus asymptomatic plaque; this does not establish methylation as the cause of lower KIF13B.
Results: Decreased expression of KIF13B in VSMCs is linked to the progression of atherosclerosis in humans; Figure 1; Supplemental Figure 1; Methods: Human studies.

documents.title: Vascular smooth muscle cell-derived KIF13B inhibits proinflammatory responses to protect against atherosclerosis
documents.text:
VSMC-specific Kif13b deletion worsened experimental atherosclerotic lesion and plaque-stability phenotypes in male AAV8-PCSK9 mice without detected differences in plasma total cholesterol or triglycerides in the tested model.
This supports a causal VSMC contribution in this mouse model; it does not establish a universally lipid-independent mechanism in humans.
Model
Male Kif13b floxed and VSMC-specific Kif13b-KO mice received AAV8-PCSK9-D377Y and Western diet for 20 weeks; major comparisons n=8 per group.
Plaque phenotype
Kif13b loss increased aortic and aortic-root lesion burden, necrotic-core area, CD68-positive macrophage accumulation and TUNEL-positive cells, while reducing collagen and plaque-stability features.
Plasma lipids
No detected genotype difference in plasma total cholesterol or triglycerides was reported in the primary Western-diet comparison.
Vascular function
Phenylephrine-induced aortic-ring contraction was impaired with VSMC Kif13b loss; n=4 per group.
Results: Depletion of Kif13b in VSMCs exacerbates atherosclerosis in mice; Figure 2.

documents.title: Vascular smooth muscle cell-derived KIF13B inhibits proinflammatory responses to protect against atherosclerosis
documents.text:
The pooled mouse aortic single-cell comparison linked KIF13B loss to a shift from matrix/collagen-associated VSMC-derived states toward inflammatory programs.
Five mice were pooled into one library per genotype, limiting independent library-level replication. Figure captions also contain unresolved duration and cluster-label inconsistencies, so this page reports the robust program-level conclusion rather than over-resolving ambiguous subpanel labels.
Single-cell design
Ldlr-deficient and Ldlr-deficient Kif13b-deficient aortas used five pooled mice to create one single-cell sample per genotype.
Cell-state programs
KIF13B loss was associated with reduced extracellular-matrix/collagen programs and increased apoptosis/inflammatory programs, with fewer matrix-associated VSMC-Fib states and more inflammatory VSMC-Fib states.
Duration discrepancy
Figure 5 and Results describe 20 weeks of Western diet; Figure 6 SCENIC and Figure 7 integrative captions reference 12 weeks. The discrepancy is retained rather than resolved.
Cluster-label discrepancy
Results assign the inflammatory Ccl2/Il1b/Il6/Il18/Trap1 signal to VSMC-Fib4, while Figure 5K caption labels the panel VSMC-Fib1; no unqualified cluster-specific gene claim is made here.
Results: Inhibiting KIF13B promotes proinflammatory fibroblast-like VSMC transition; Figures 5-7.

documents.title: Vascular smooth muscle cell-derived KIF13B inhibits proinflammatory responses to protect against atherosclerosis
documents.text:
KIF13B gain- and loss-of-function directly altered matrix, inflammatory and contractile phenotypes in primary human aortic smooth muscle cells under oxLDL.
These are cell-autonomous in vitro perturbation experiments and do not demonstrate a patient treatment effect.
KIF13B knockdown
Knockdown reduced TAGLN, collagen secretion and collagen-gel contraction while increasing fibroblast/inflammatory features; Western/ELISA assays generally n=3 and gel contraction n=5.
KIF13B overexpression
Overexpression produced reciprocal matrix/contractile effects; Western/ELISA assays generally n=3 and gel contraction n=6.
Results: Inhibiting KIF13B promotes proinflammatory fibroblast-like VSMC transition; Figure 5L-Q and Supplemental Figure 3.

documents.title: Vascular smooth muscle cell-derived KIF13B inhibits proinflammatory responses to protect against atherosclerosis
documents.text:
KLF4 functionally mediated KIF13B-loss-associated VSMC reprogramming in primary HASMC experiments.
The rescue establishes a downstream functional relationship in this experimental system, not a causal human clinical mechanism.
KLF4 response
KIF13B knockdown increased KLF4 protein, whereas KIF13B overexpression decreased it; Western blot n=3 and selected immunofluorescence n=10.
Genetic rescue
Concomitant KLF4 knockdown rescued KIF13B-loss-associated reductions in collagen/matrix markers and increases in inflammatory factors; Western, qPCR and ELISA assays n=3.
Results: KLF4 mediates KIF13B-dependent proinflammatory VSMC reprogramming; Figure 6.

documents.title: Vascular smooth muscle cell-derived KIF13B inhibits proinflammatory responses to protect against atherosclerosis
documents.text:
Proteostasis and rescue experiments support KCTD10-dependent KLF4 ubiquitination and proteasomal turnover downstream of KIF13B.
Molecular docking was predictive, while KCTD10-KLF4 association, ubiquitination and rescue were experimentally evaluated. The upstream mechanism by which KIF13B maintains KCTD10 abundance remains unresolved.
KLF4 turnover
CHX chase, MG132 and KLF4 ubiquitination assays showed that KIF13B knockdown stabilized KLF4 by attenuating proteasomal degradation; n=3 independent biological replicates.
KCTD10 identification
Integrated mouse VSMC and human unstable/stable plaque transcriptomics nominated KCTD10 and SKP1; KIF13B perturbation altered KCTD10 rather than SKP1 in HASMC protein assays.
KCTD10-KLF4 mechanism
Docking predicted interaction; co-IP supported KCTD10-KLF4 association, KCTD10 overexpression increased KLF4 ubiquitination and reduced KLF4 protein.
KCTD10 rescue
KCTD10 overexpression reversed KIF13B-knockdown-associated KLF4 stabilization and rescued collagen/inflammatory phenotypes.
Results: KIF13B facilitates KCTD10-mediated ubiquitination and degradation of KLF4; Figures 7-8 and Supplemental Figure 4.

documents.title: Vascular smooth muscle cell-derived KIF13B inhibits proinflammatory responses to protect against atherosclerosis
documents.text:
Kenpaullone reduced KLF4 promoter activity/expression and produced preclinical rescue of KIF13B-loss-associated cellular and mouse plaque phenotypes.
Kenpaullone is not established as a KLF4-selective drug. Authoritative pharmacology sources describe it as an ATP-competitive CDK/GSK3β inhibitor. The rescue therefore supports preclinical pathway modulation but does not prove KLF4-selective pharmacology or human treatment efficacy.
Cell intervention
Kenpaullone at 10 µM reduced KLF4 and rescued collagen/inflammatory phenotypes after KIF13B knockdown in HASMCs; n=3 biological replicates for key Western/ELISA assays.
Mouse intervention
Male PCSK9 mice received oral Kenpaullone 1 mg/kg/day for the final 12 weeks of a 20-week Western-diet protocol; n=6 per group.
Mouse outcomes
Kenpaullone reduced measured inflammatory cytokines, lesion burden, necrotic-core area, CD68-positive macrophages and TUNEL-positive cells and increased collagen.
Measured safety-related endpoints
No detected changes were reported in measured body weight, plasma TC/TG or ALT/AST endpoints; these measurements do not establish general or human safety.
Results: Pharmacological inhibition of KLF4 with Kenpaullone alleviates atherosclerosis in mice; Figure 9 and Supplemental Figures 5-7.

documents.title: Vascular smooth muscle cell-derived KIF13B inhibits proinflammatory responses to protect against atherosclerosis
documents.text:
What is the human evidence linking KIF13B to atherosclerotic plaque severity?
Paired carotid endarterectomy tissue and independent human transcriptomic and proteomic datasets showed lower KIF13B in more advanced or unstable plaque states, with prominent VSMC differences and lower collagen in advanced local plaque regions. These are associative human observations and do not establish that manipulating KIF13B changes plaque outcomes in patients.

documents.title: Vascular smooth muscle cell-derived KIF13B inhibits proinflammatory responses to protect against atherosclerosis
documents.text:
Did VSMC-specific Kif13b deletion cause worse atherosclerosis in mice?
In the tested male AAV8-PCSK9 model, VSMC-specific Kif13b deletion increased lesion burden, necrotic core, macrophage accumulation and apoptotic-cell signal and reduced collagen/plaque-stability features. No genotype difference in measured plasma total cholesterol or triglycerides was detected in the primary comparison.

documents.title: Vascular smooth muscle cell-derived KIF13B inhibits proinflammatory responses to protect against atherosclerosis
documents.text:
What did the single-cell experiment show, and were there five independent replicates per genotype?
The pooled aortic single-cell comparison associated KIF13B loss with reduced matrix/collagen programs and increased inflammatory VSMC-derived programs. Five mice were pooled into one single-cell library per genotype, so the design does not provide five independent scRNA-seq libraries per group.

documents.title: Vascular smooth muscle cell-derived KIF13B inhibits proinflammatory responses to protect against atherosclerosis
documents.text:
Why does this page not assign one definitive diet duration to all single-cell analyses?
The Results and Figure 5 describe the generated aortic single-cell experiment after 20 weeks of Western diet, whereas Figure 6 SCENIC and Figure 7 integrative captions reference 12 weeks. The evidence page preserves this source discrepancy instead of silently harmonizing it.

documents.title: Vascular smooth muscle cell-derived KIF13B inhibits proinflammatory responses to protect against atherosclerosis
documents.text:
How does KIF13B affect primary human vascular smooth muscle cells?
Under oxLDL, KIF13B knockdown reduced contractile/matrix features, collagen secretion and collagen-gel contraction and increased inflammatory features, while KIF13B overexpression produced reciprocal effects. These are in vitro primary-HASMC perturbation data, not human treatment outcomes.

documents.title: Vascular smooth muscle cell-derived KIF13B inhibits proinflammatory responses to protect against atherosclerosis
documents.text:
Is KLF4 functionally downstream of KIF13B?
In primary HASMC experiments, KIF13B loss increased KLF4, and concomitant KLF4 knockdown rescued the collagen-suppressive and inflammatory phenotype caused by KIF13B knockdown. This supports a downstream functional relationship in the tested cell system.

documents.title: Vascular smooth muscle cell-derived KIF13B inhibits proinflammatory responses to protect against atherosclerosis
documents.text:
What evidence supports the KIF13B-KCTD10-KLF4 mechanism?
KIF13B knockdown stabilized KLF4 in CHX/proteasome experiments and reduced KLF4 ubiquitination. Integrated analyses nominated KCTD10, co-IP supported KCTD10-KLF4 association, KCTD10 increased KLF4 ubiquitination, and KCTD10 overexpression rescued KIF13B-loss phenotypes. The study does not resolve how KIF13B itself controls KCTD10 abundance.

documents.title: Vascular smooth muscle cell-derived KIF13B inhibits proinflammatory responses to protect against atherosclerosis
documents.text:
Does Kenpaullone prove that KLF4 is a clinically validated treatment target for atherosclerosis?
No. Kenpaullone reduced KLF4 promoter activity/expression and rescued cellular and mouse phenotypes in this study, but the experiments were preclinical. Kenpaullone is also a pharmacologically nonselective kinase inhibitor rather than an established KLF4-selective clinical drug, and no human atherosclerosis treatment efficacy or safety was tested.

documents.title: Vascular smooth muscle cell-derived KIF13B inhibits proinflammatory responses to protect against atherosclerosis
documents.text:
How does this JCI study differ from the European Heart Journal KIF13B study?
The JCI study focuses on vascular smooth muscle cells and a KIF13B-KCTD10-KLF4 mechanism controlling matrix/inflammatory VSMC states. The European Heart Journal study focuses on macrophage KIF13B, MERTK-dependent efferocytosis and an ITCH/CBL regulatory network. Together they describe distinct cell-type-specific KIF13B mechanisms in experimental atherosclerosis.

documents.title: Vascular smooth muscle cell-derived KIF13B inhibits proinflammatory responses to protect against atherosclerosis
documents.text:
Which public datasets and repositories support this evidence page?
Key resources include study-generated mouse single-cell data GSE314838, human stable/unstable carotid plaque RNA-seq GSE120521, human plaque proteomics PXD062283, public spatial-transcriptomic evidence associated with GSE274572, the article's public methylation datasets, the JCI Supplemental Data, and the Supporting Data Values file.

documents.title: Vascular smooth muscle cell-derived KIF13B inhibits proinflammatory responses to protect against atherosclerosis
documents.text:
What evidence links VSMC-derived KIF13B to atherosclerosis and plaque stability?
Human plaque KIF13B associations and VSMC-specific mouse deletion support different evidence levels; only the mouse intervention is causal in its model.

documents.title: Vascular smooth muscle cell-derived KIF13B inhibits proinflammatory responses to protect against atherosclerosis
documents.text:
How does KIF13B affect inflammatory and matrix-associated VSMC states?
Pooled mouse single-cell analysis and primary HASMC perturbation link KIF13B to inflammatory and matrix-associated VSMC programs.

documents.title: Vascular smooth muscle cell-derived KIF13B inhibits proinflammatory responses to protect against atherosclerosis
documents.text:
What evidence places KLF4 downstream of KIF13B in vascular smooth muscle cells?
KLF4 functional rescue in primary HASMCs supports a downstream relationship in that experimental system.

documents.title: Vascular smooth muscle cell-derived KIF13B inhibits proinflammatory responses to protect against atherosclerosis
documents.text:
How does KCTD10 contribute to KIF13B-dependent regulation of KLF4?
Proteostasis and rescue experiments support KCTD10-dependent KLF4 turnover; upstream control of KCTD10 remains unresolved.

documents.title: Vascular smooth muscle cell-derived KIF13B inhibits proinflammatory responses to protect against atherosclerosis
documents.text:
What preclinical rescue evidence was reported using Kenpaullone?
Kenpaullone altered KLF4-related readouts and rescued cellular and mouse phenotypes preclinically; it is not established as a KLF4-selective human drug.

documents.text:
Association between lower KIF13B and more advanced or unstable human atherosclerotic plaque features across local tissue and independent public datasets.
A causal contribution of VSMC Kif13b loss to measured atherosclerotic plaque phenotypes in the tested male mouse models.
Cell-autonomous effects of KIF13B gain and loss on matrix, inflammatory and contractile programs in primary HASMCs.
Functional placement of KLF4 downstream of KIF13B in HASMC perturbation and rescue experiments.

documents.text:
That low KIF13B expression or KIF13B methylation causes plaque instability in humans.
That KIF13B, KCTD10, KLF4 or Kenpaullone has proven therapeutic efficacy or safety in patients with atherosclerosis.
That Kenpaullone is selective for KLF4 or that all Kenpaullone effects in this study are mediated specifically through KLF4.
A universal lipid-independent KIF13B mechanism in humans; the reported absence of TC/TG differences applies to the tested mouse comparison.
Independent replication of the study-generated single-cell comparison, because five mice were pooled into one library per genotype.

Generalization of the causal or pharmacologic mouse findings to females, because only male mice were used.

documents.title: Vascular smooth muscle cell-derived KIF13B inhibits proinflammatory responses to protect against atherosclerosis
documents.text:
The local human cohort contained six carotid endarterectomy patients with paired within-plaque regions; human observations are associative and small-sample.
The local advanced-versus-adjacent classification was based on anatomical location and macroscopic surgical appearance rather than molecular or histopathological criteria.
Stable/unstable public datasets and local advanced/adjacent paired regions use different plaque definitions and should not be treated as interchangeable cohorts.
Human methylation observations are associative and do not establish that KIF13B hypermethylation causes KIF13B downregulation or plaque instability.
The PXD062283 repository contains 87 plaques overall, whereas the JCI stable/unstable comparison uses a subset of 19 and 38; repository size and analytical subset must not be conflated.
Five mice were pooled into one single-cell library per genotype, limiting independent biological replication at the single-cell library level.
Figure 5/Results report a 20-week Western-diet single-cell experiment, whereas downstream Figure 6/7 captions reference 12 weeks; this discrepancy is unresolved.
Results describe inflammatory genes in VSMC-Fib4 while the Figure 5K caption labels the panel VSMC-Fib1; the evidence page therefore avoids treating that subpanel label as unambiguous.
Only male mice were used, and sex was not analyzed as a biological variable.
Tagln-Cre targets smooth-muscle compartments beyond plaque VSMCs; reported intestine/bladder measurements do not establish general systemic safety of pathway targeting.
The study establishes KCTD10-dependent KLF4 ubiquitination/rescue evidence but does not identify the mechanism by which KIF13B regulates KCTD10 abundance.
Kenpaullone is pharmacologically nonselective; its rescue does not prove KLF4-selective target engagement or exclude contributions from other kinase targets.
Kenpaullone was evaluated only in cells and mice. No human atherosclerosis efficacy, dosing, pharmacokinetic or safety trial was performed.

documents.title: A Multimodal artificial intelligence framework for mechanistic discovery and digital twin construction in cardiovascular medicine
documents.text:
This Correspondence discusses a research agenda connecting multimodal biological interpretation with patient-specific simulation in cardiovascular medicine. It sets out design and translation requirements without reporting a newly built, clinically validated digital twin system.
The Correspondence outlines two linked directions for cardiovascular AI: investigating disease mechanisms and developing patient-specific digital twins. It discusses combining imaging and molecular information to generate network and disease-subtyping hypotheses, then considers updateable physiological models, image-to-mesh workflows and treatment-scenario simulation. Longitudinal data, computational capacity, prospective evaluation, privacy and governance are presented as requirements for translation. This page organizes those narrative arguments for research planning and methodological citation. The cited empirical examples remain evidence from other works; cross-modal integration does not itself establish causation, and simulated treatment scenarios are not observed therapeutic effects in patients.

What design, sample and mortality follow-up were used?
The NHANES 2007–2018 analytic sample included 5,837 participants and 906 deaths, with a mean follow-up of 6.5 years and survey-weighted Cox analysis. Raw participant counts and survey-weighted percentages are different quantities and must not be directly substituted for one another.

documents.text:
How was short sleep associated with mortality?
In fully adjusted Model 3, short sleep (<7 h versus 7–9 h) was associated with all-cause mortality at HR 1.25 (95% CI 1.04–1.51). This is an observational association, not a randomized intervention that shortens or extends sleep.

Restricted cubic splines showed nonlinearity (P<0.001), with an estimated sleep-duration turning point of 7.23 h. The turning point is a model estimate from this dataset, not an intervention-validated sleep prescription or a precise target for every individual.

documents.title: Association between sleep duration, sleep trouble and all-cause mortality in individuals with hyperuricemia in the United States
documents.text:
What mortality evidence relates sleep duration to hyperuricemia?
In 5,837 NHANES participants with hyperuricemia, with 906 deaths and mean follow-up of 6.5 years, Model 3 associations were HR 1.25 (95% CI 1.04–1.51) for <7 h and HR 1.50 (95% CI 1.10–2.04) for >9 h versus 7–9 h. These survey-weighted associations are not intervention effects or individual absolute-risk estimates.

documents.title: Association between sleep duration, sleep trouble and all-cause mortality in individuals with hyperuricemia in the United States
documents.text:
What does survey-weighted NHANES analysis contribute?
The 2007–2018 linked-mortality analytic sample comprised 5,837 participants and 906 deaths with mean follow-up of 6.5 years. Survey-weighted Cox analysis does not make raw counts interchangeable with weighted percentages.

documents.title: Association between sleep duration, sleep trouble and all-cause mortality in individuals with hyperuricemia in the United States
documents.text:
Was self-reported sleep trouble independently associated with mortality?
Model 3 gave HR 1.04 (95% CI 0.87–1.25), P=0.651, without a statistically significant association for the self-reported indicator. This cannot be generalized to all diagnosed sleep disorders.

Restricted cubic splines gave nonlinearity P<0.001 and an estimated turning point of 7.23 h. This dataset-specific model estimate is not an intervention-validated prescription.

documents.title: Deciphering the Proteomic Landscape of Circulating Extracellular Vesicles in Human Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm
documents.text: Can targeted circulating extracellular-vesicle protein profiling identify AAA-associated candidates that merit external assay evaluation, and how consistent are their signals across Western blot, ELISA and ROC analyses?

documents.title: Deciphering the Proteomic Landscape of Circulating Extracellular Vesicles in Human Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm
documents.text:
A two-center exploratory study profiled 92 circulating EV-associated proteins in AAA and evaluated five candidates by Western blot and ELISA. External sample size, assay-dependent expression differences and wide ROC uncertainty are retained explicitly.
This two-center human study enrolled 18 AAA patients and 9 healthy controls: 10 cases and 5 controls in the in-house cohort, and 8 cases and 4 controls in the external cohort. A targeted Olink proximity-extension workflow assessed 92 EV-associated proteins and prioritized five candidates. External Western blot and ELISA did not show uniformly concordant findings: MCP-1 direction differed between the two reported analyses, and Neurturin was not significant by Western blot but lower by ELISA. The article reports single-marker ROC AUCs from 0.760 to 0.900 in the small external comparison, with wide confidence intervals. Different passages also describe venous plasma, serum EVs and intraoperative aortic blood; those specimen descriptions are not silently treated as one validated routine blood-screening protocol. The evidence is exploratory biomarker association and external assay assessment, not prospective AAA detection, rupture prediction or a therapeutic target validation.

documents.title: Machine learning combined with omics-based approaches reveals T-lymphocyte cellular fate imbalance in abdominal aortic aneurysm
documents.text:
Integrated human single-cell and bulk transcriptomic analyses describe AAA-associated T-cell state heterogeneity, derive TIRS and evaluate candidate biomarkers in public datasets and small independent human samples, with supportive mouse expression evidence.
The study combined human AAA single-cell profiles, public bulk transcriptomic cohorts and independent clinical samples to describe T-cell heterogeneity and infer transcriptional state relationships. Four aneurysmal aortic samples yielded 7,343 post-QC cells, including 3,841 T cells assigned to eight phenotypes. Monocle inferred a branching trajectory; it did not directly follow individual cells over time. Integrative gene-set analysis derived a 50-gene TIRS, and LASSO plus SVM-RFE prioritized FOSB, JUNB, CST7 and TBC1D4. Marker discrimination varied across public cohorts and was evaluated in small independent aortic-wall samples (5 AAA, 4 controls) and peripheral blood (24 AAA, 15 controls). BAPN + AngII mouse experiments provided supportive FOSB/JUNB expression evidence. These findings support transcriptomic associations and candidate-marker evaluation, while prospective diagnostic utility, human causal mechanisms and treatment benefit remain unestablished.

Yes: aortic wall from 5 AAA and 4 controls, and peripheral blood from 24 AAA and 15 controls. Aortic-wall AUCs were 1.000/1.000/0.600/0.800 and blood AUCs were 0.989/0.906/0.933/0.736 in FOSB/JUNB/CST7/TBC1D4 order. The aortic-wall sample was small.

documents.title: Targeted Delivery of Exosome-Derived miRNA-185-5p Inhibitor via Liposomes Alleviates Apoptosis and Cuproptosis in Dilated Cardiomyopathy
documents.text:
A preclinical study evaluated peptide-functionalized miR-185-5p-inhibitor liposomes in DOX-injured cells and mice, with formulation, biodistribution, cardiac phenotyping and cell-death-associated readouts. No human therapeutic efficacy was established.
This preclinical investigation assessed miR-185-5p-inhibitor-loaded liposomes in doxorubicin (DOX)-injured H9C2 cells, human iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes in vitro and male C57BL/6 mouse models. The delivery vehicle is a peptide-functionalized liposome, not a clinical infusion of patient-derived exosomes. Loaded particles had a reported DLS diameter of 172.35 ± 0.8 nm and encapsulation efficiency of 98.0 ± 1.2%; TEM and DLS size measurements represent different measurement contexts. Mouse experiments reported greater cardiac fluorescence with the targeting peptide and improvements in echocardiographic and histological readouts. Cell experiments assessed apoptosis- and cuproptosis-associated proteins and other injury signals. These findings support the tested preclinical delivery strategy; they do not establish human efficacy, human safety, a general DCM therapy or complete pathway-specific causality. Abstract-only survival/percentage claims and unresolved protocol-reporting details are not promoted into independently verified quantitative key findings.

documents.title: Targeting the NLRP3 inflammasome abrogates cardiotoxicity of immune checkpoint blockers
documents.text: Does NLRP3 inflammasome inhibition mitigate immune-checkpoint-inhibitor cardiac injury while reshaping cardiac immune-cell states and preserving or enhancing antitumor activity in the tested preclinical melanoma models?

documents.title: Targeting the NLRP3 inflammasome abrogates cardiotoxicity of immune checkpoint blockers
documents.text:
A preclinical multimodal study evaluates MCC950 in B16F10-bearing mouse models of ICI-associated cardiac injury, combining cardiac and tumor phenotyping with immune profiling and supportive public human PBMC association data.
The study tested NLRP3 inhibition with MCC950 in female C57BL/6J mice bearing B16F10 melanoma during anti-PD-1 or dual anti-PD-1 plus anti-CTLA-4 treatment. Cardiac biomarkers, echocardiography, histology, immune profiling and transcriptomics supported preclinical effects on cardiac injury and inflammatory states. Cardiac single-cell analysis comprised 68,058 cells from a pooled design with six hearts per sample; these cells are not independent mouse replicates. MCC950 altered macrophage and T-cell states, and the experiments included macrophage depletion, a dual-ICI comparison with n=8 per group, and a mouse treatment-after-injury protocol. Public GSE180045 human PBMC data supplied supportive NLRP3/IL1B associations only. Cardiac and tumor effects in these mouse models do not establish human treatment efficacy, safety or approved clinical use.

What model was used to study ICI cardiotoxicity?

Human tissue observations are associative; causal and pharmacologic tests are preclinical.

documents.title: The macrophage-derived motor protein KIF13B enhances MERTK-mediated efferocytosis and prevents atherosclerosis in mice
documents.text:
A mechanistic translational preclinical study linking myeloid KIF13B to MERTK-dependent efferocytosis and experimental plaque protection, with associative human tissue evidence and article-reported NX-1607 rescue in cells and mice.
The study combined associative human arterial and carotid-plaque observations with mouse atherosclerosis genetics, public and study-generated single-cell/transcriptomic analyses, macrophage experiments, genetic rescue and preclinical pharmacologic intervention. KIF13B expression was lower in advanced human arterial/plaque tissue and progressing mouse plaques. Global Kif13b loss worsened atherosclerosis in Ldlr-deficient mice but increased circulating lipids in that model. Myeloid-specific deletion and Kif13b-deficient bone-marrow transplantation worsened lesion burden, necrotic cores, macrophage and apoptotic-cell accumulation without corresponding plasma-lipid changes, supporting a local myeloid/hematopoietic contribution in mice. Kif13b-deficient macrophages showed impaired efferocytosis and lower MERTK protein; restoring MERTK in deficient BMDMs improved efferocytosis. Unchanged Mertk mRNA, reduced MERTK protein stability, proteasome dependence, increased MERTK ubiquitination, KIF13B/ITCH interaction and ITCH/CBL/MERTK rescue results support a post-translational regulatory model, although the exact proposed ITCH-mediated CBL degradation step remains incompletely demonstrated. The article reported that NX-1607 improved MERTK/efferocytosis phenotypes in macrophages and reduced atherosclerotic phenotypes in mice. The article describes NX-1607 as a CBL inhibitor, whereas external authoritative drug-development sources identify it as a CBL-B/CBLB inhibitor; CBL and CBLB are distinct genes. Thus NX-1607 is reported as preclinical pharmacologic rescue, not unambiguous target validation of endogenous CBL. No human atherosclerosis treatment efficacy was tested.
